description: Interested in visualizing trends in air pollutant concentration, join.
summary: System Trend Houdini is a statistical “trend detective” for air pollution in Guatemala’s metropolitan area. We combined 84 months (2018–2025) of satellite nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) data from Copernicus Sentinel-5P/TROPOMI with NASA data: OMI NO₂ for a regional baseline, MERRA-2 wind, and GPM IMERG rainfall. Using Mann-Kendall and Sen’s slope tests, we found that NO₂ in the metro area is rising by about 3.2% per year (p = 0.0024), much faster than the regional trend (+0.4% per year). Wind has only a weak effect, rainfall none, and the CA-9 Sur hotspot is not statistically significant, so we report the limits of the evidence honestly. This answers the challenge by separating a real Earth system trend from seasonal and weather noise. It matters because NO₂ comes from traffic and industry and can harm respiratory health, so knowing whether it is truly rising helps people and decision-makers act. Our open Streamlit dashboard and repository let anyone explore and reproduce the evidence.
details:
What it does and how it works. System Trend Houdini tests whether nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) pollution in Guatemala’s Metropolitan Area (AMG) is truly rising or just fluctuating. We built a monthly NO₂ series for July 2018 to June 2025 (84 months) from Copernicus Sentinel-5P/TROPOMI. We compared it with NASA OMI (Aura) NO₂ for a regional baseline, and with NASA MERRA-2 wind and GPM IMERG rainfall for weather context. A Python statistics engine runs a Mann-Kendall trend test, Sen’s slope and Pearson correlations. Results feed a live Streamlit dashboard (Trend Detective · AMG) and a web scroll-story.

Results and benefits. NO₂ in the AMG is rising about 3.18% per year (p = 0.0024), much faster than the regional OMI trend (+0.40% per year). Wind shows a weak negative link (r = −0.224, p = 0.041), rainfall is not significant (p = 0.110), and the CA-9 Sur corridor hotspot is not significant on its own (p = 0.111). The benefit is a clear, quantified answer with honest limits, instead of an impression from a noisy chart.

Intended impact. We want local decision-makers, researchers and citizens to have open, reproducible evidence on air quality in a city where it matters, and a method other cities can copy by changing the area of interest.

Tools and technology.

Languages: Python (data processing, statistics and dashboard), JavaScript/HTML/CSS (web scroll-story), Jupyter notebooks.
Data processing and analysis: numpy, pandas, SciPy, pymannkendall (Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope), xarray and rioxarray (satellite rasters and data cubes), GeoPandas and Shapely (geospatial processing of the metropolitan area boundary).
Visualization: Matplotlib and seaborn (maps and charts), Plotly (interactive charts), Folium and pydeck (map exploration), windrose (wind analysis), imageio (month-by-month animation).
Dashboards and web: Streamlit and Streamlit Community Cloud (live dashboard and hosting), React (loaded from a CDN) with hand-drawn SVG for the scroll-story web page.
Data access and formats: NASA Giovanni (OMI NO₂), Sentinel Hub Python client (Sentinel-5P/TROPOMI), CSV and GeoJSON files.
Development: GitHub for version control and the open repository

Creativity. We treat the problem as a “trend detective” case: the dashboard ends in a statistical verdict, not just charts. We also report what did not hold up, such as the hotspot and rainfall results. A month-by-month animated map and a scroll-story make the evidence readable for non-specialists, and a built-in glossary explains the statistics.

Factors we considered. Seasonality and weather noise, which is why we used a non-parametric trend test. Confounders such as wind dispersion and rain washout. Coarse satellite grid resolution. Missing months in the hotspot series (73 of 84 months). Cross-checking the local trend against the regional OMI series. And reproducibility: all data recipes, notebooks and code are open in our repository.
